content: Welcome to Latin.
This pack teaches one skill: reading. You
will look at a printed line and know what
it says. Nothing here asks you to compose
Latin of your own.
Every card carries a word, a short
sentence that uses it, and a few notes.
Lessons like this one arrive on the card
that first needs them.
Latin is printed in the alphabet you
already read, and almost every letter
says what an English reader expects.
Four do not. This pack reads them as
Caesar's Rome did — the restored sounds
— and pages 4 and 5 are the list.
Latin cards keep a grey cue where a German
course prints der or die. It is not an
article but the dictionary entry, shortened:
m., -is  rēx  =  rēx, rēgis, masculine
Nouns cue gender and the genitive ending
(f., -ae = puella, puellae). Verbs cue the
infinitive that names the conjugation:
-āre, -ēre, -ere, -īre. Adjectives cue
three endings, -us, -a, -um. irreg. means
more than one stem. A bare infinitive like
sequī means a verb with no active forms.
What you memorize is the headword with its
macrons AND the cue: together they are the
dictionary form. The Notes spell the
genitive out. The voice says the word alone.
The noun cue gives two things: gender,
and the genitive ending. That ending
sorts every noun into one of five
families, the declensions:
f., -ae   puella, puellae     1st
m., -ī    lēgātus, lēgātī     2nd
n., -ī    sīgnum, sīgnī       2nd
m., -is   cōnsul, cōnsulis    3rd
m., -ūs   senātus, senātūs    4th
f., -eī   rēs, reī            5th
Any gender rides in front: f., -is urbs,
n., -is tempus, m./f., -eī diēs. The
fifth also writes -ēī: aciēs, aciēī.
senātus and lēgātus both end in -us; only
the genitive tells the 4th from the 2nd.
Before e or i, English softens c and g.
Latin never does — they stay hard
everywhere:
c = 'k' as in cat, always        Press 1
cīvis — KEE-wiss, 'citizen'
g = 'g' as in got, always        Press 2
genus — GEH-noos, 'kind, race'
One name is worth reading right from the
start, because it is on almost every card:
Caesar — KY-sar               Press 3
Said aloud it is the German Kaiser: the
emperors kept Caesar's own sound. The ae
is Lesson 3's story.
The other two never vary at all:
v = 'w' as in wine               Press 1
via — WEE-ah, 'road'
qu = 'qu' as in quick            Press 2
aqua — AH-kwah, 'water'
Latin v is the sound English writes as
w — wine itself is vīnum, borrowed early.
That is the whole list of letters that
catch an English reader out. Everything
else reads close enough to its spelling.
Recognition only: you are learning what
a printed word sounds like, not how to
spell one from the sound.
A line over a vowel — ā ē ī ō ū — is a
macron. It marks one thing: hold that
vowel a little longer. The sound does not
change, the way English 'moon' holds its
vowel longer than 'book'.
rēs — RAYSS, the ē held out      Press 1
'thing, matter'
It keeps words spelled alike apart: hic
('this') and hīc ('here'), malum ('bad')
and mālum ('an apple'). It also draws the
stress onto itself in the second-last
syllable: a thing to notice, not to solve.
The cards print macrons on the headword, as
every Latin dictionary does. The sentences
leave them off, as real Latin texts do.
English marks a word's job by where it
stands. 'The dog bites the man' is not
'the man bites the dog', and nothing but
the order says so.
Latin marks the job on the word itself.
The ending says whether a word is the
subject, the object, or something else,
so the order is left free:
Caesar Brūtum videt.
Brūtum Caesar videt.
Videt Brūtum Caesar.
All three say Caesar sees Brutus. The
-um is what makes Brutus the one seen,
wherever in the line he stands.
Each job has a name. One of them carries
everything here: the NOMINATIVE, the
form a subject takes.
It is also the form printed on every
card and listed in every dictionary, so
you have been reading nominatives since
the first card of the pack.
Is Caesar est.   = He is Caesar.
Ego Caesar sum.  = I am Caesar.
Four further roles arrive later in the
course, one at a time, until the whole
set is in view.
Recognition only: reading a job off an
ending, never building one.
sum is the verb 'to be', and the most
common word on a Latin page. It ties a
subject to whatever is said about it,
and Latin needs nothing else to have a
whole sentence:
Rōma est.        = Rome exists.
Ego Caesar sum.  = I am Caesar.
Four shapes do nearly all of its work:
sum  = I am        es = you are
est  = he/she/it is
sunt = they are
They share no visible stem. Take them as
four whole words, known on sight.

title: LESSON 2: WHEN I ACTS LIKE Y

content: At the front of a word, an i with a
vowel behind it is not a vowel of its
own. It glides, like the y in yes.
i + vowel = 'y' as in yes        Press 1
iam — YAHM, 'already'
One syllable, not two: iam rhymes with
'yam', never 'ee-am'.
The same glide turns up between two
vowels inside a word — maior reads
MAH-yor, not MAH-ee-or.
Recognition only: spotting where i is
doing a consonant's work.
One near miss is worth naming. In the
languages Latin fathered, t before i
turned to a hiss — nation, ration.
Latin itself never did. The t stays a
plain t, wherever it stands:
-ti- = 'tee', as written         Press 1
ratiō — RAH-tee-oh, 'reason'
grātia, nātiō, ōrātiō: read them all
with the t of 'tip'.
The hiss belongs to the daughters, not
the mother — nothing on a Latin page
ever spells it.
Latin ch is not the ch of chip. It is a
plain k with a puff of breath behind it
— Greek loanwords brought it in.
ch = 'k' as in kit               Press 1
pulcher — POOL-ker, 'beautiful'
A plain c is already k, from Lesson 1,
so ch changes nothing an ear would miss:
read both as k on sight.
ae and oe are each one gliding vowel,
spoken in a single breath.
ae = 'eye', as in Kaiser         Press 1
saepe — SYE-peh, 'often'
oe = 'oy' as in boy              Press 2
poena — POY-nah, 'penalty'
Caesar from Lesson 1 is both rules in
one word: KY-sar — the c hard, the ae
an eye. So is caelum, 'sky': KY-loom.
A diphthong counts as long already, so
it never carries a macron.
Most nouns wear their family plainly.
A few do not, and the cue is where the
warning sits.
vir is cued m., -rī. Nothing on it ends
-us, but the genitive virī puts it in
the second declension all the same. ager
and puer go with it, and in ager the e
drops out: ager, agrī.
Gender can surprise. collēga and poēta
end in -a and take -ae like puella, yet
they are men: the cue reads m., -ae.
humus goes the other way, cued f., -ī —
second declension, feminine.
A noun in -ium doubles its i: convīvium
is cued n., -iī.
Some nouns have no singular at all. The
cue then gives the genitive PLURAL, and
the word is read as a plural always:
n., -um     castra, castrōrum
n., -um     arma, armōrum
m., -um     līberī, līberōrum
f., -ārum   īnsidiae, īnsidiārum
f., -um     dīvitiae, dīvitiārum
castra is one camp, not many; arma is
the gear a man fights in; līberī is the
children of a single house. Latin counts
each as a set, so the form stays plural
where English says one thing.
Read -um and -ārum here as genitive
plurals, never as a singular ending.
Connectives are not filler. Each one
says what the sentence is about to do,
and Latin uses them from the first line
a reader ever meets.
et    = and
atque = and, and what is more
sed   = but, and here is the turn
nōn   = not, a flat denial
Nōn est meus, sed tuus est.
= He is not mine, but yours.
nōn ... sed ... is a fixed pair, 'not X
but Y'. Catching the pair is half of
reading the sentence.
-que is the odd one out. It means 'and',
but it is not a separate word: it clings
to the END of the second thing joined.
Gallia Italiaque
= Gaul and Italy
Read that as Italia + que. The word it
hangs on is the word it drags in.
It binds more tightly than et, which is
why fixed pairs use it: senātus
populusque Rōmānus.
Recognition of function only: what a
connective says is happening, never how
to place one yourself.

title: LESSON 8: THE LINKS: WHEN AND IF

content: Lesson 7's joints hold two statements
side by side. These hang one clause off
another:
cum  = when, since
ut   = as; so that
sī   = if
quod = because; the fact that
nisi = unless
Sī hoc vērum est...
= If this is true...
Each announces the KIND of clause on its
way before the clause itself arrives.
That warning is what they are for.
Three more carry an argument forward:
enim   = for (gives the reason)
nam    = for, since
igitur = therefore (draws a result)
Three fix a point in time:
iam  = already      tum = then
nunc = now
None of these adds a new thing to
picture. They say how the next piece of
the sentence stands to the one before.
Recognition only: naming what is coming,
not building a clause.
Five verbs turn up on nearly every page
of Latin, and not one of them is
regular. They sit here because they are
common, not because they are orderly.
possum = be able, can
volō   = want, wish
eō     = go
ferō   = bear, bring; endure
fīō    = become, happen
Their third-person forms are the ones a
reader actually meets:
potest, vult, it, fert, fit
possum and volō lean on a second verb in
its plain -re form: Nēmō hoc facere
potest. = No one can do this.
Nothing in fert announces ferō, and it
is a short word to catch. Take each of
these shapes as a word in its own right,
tied by memory to its headword.
possum is sum with pot- in front of it:
pot-est, pos-sumus. Lesson 1's verb is
sitting inside it.
ferō passes its shape to everything
built from it — auferō and īnferō, met
later, carry the same fert. Worth
noticing now; nothing to do with it yet.
Recognition only: knowing an odd shape
belongs to a verb already in hand.
Two verbs here are cued oddly, and both
shapes come back later.
faciō is cued -iō, -ere. The infinitive
is third-conjugation facere, but the I
form ends -iō, and that i runs on
through the verb: facit, faciunt. capiō
and accipiō are built the same way.
dō is cued dare, a whole infinitive. It
looks first-conjugation and nearly is,
but the a of dare is short, so the cue
prints the word instead of -āre. What is
built on it — circumdare — follows suit.
A bare infinitive in a cue is not always
a deponent, then. The deponents all end
in -ī: sequī, hortārī, potīrī.
